name: Sam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the local politics reporter for the regional public broadcaster, so I write for the news website and do short pieces for the radio bulletins. A normal day is a council committee in the morning, which can be three hours on bin collections and planning rules, then I write it up and record a forty-second version for the one o'clock news. In the afternoon I chase councillors for comments and try to find the one story in a two-hundred-page budget report. I like explaining how the place actually works to people who'd never read those reports.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI in that day at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit, yes. I use a transcription tool for the long council meetings, because it saves me an hour of rewinding, and now and then I ask a chatbot to summarise a dull report so I know where to look. I always check it, because it once told me a councillor voted for something she'd voted against. My partner Lena teaches at a primary school, we rent a terraced house, and we've got about four months' worth saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that the transcription tool is handy and that's about it. I'd probably joke online that the robots couldn't sit through a planning committee either. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry isn't AI in that picture, it's money. The broadcaster's budget has been frozen for three years, and every frozen year means a post doesn't get filled. Every frozen budget year means a post on our desk doesn't get filled. Our regional desk has gone from nine people to six. A hype bubble bursting doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep the transcription tool because it's genuinely useful. I'd stay active in the union branch, mostly because the next budget freeze will need a fight. Lena and I would keep putting a couple of hundred a month away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A low background hum of worry, but it's the same hum I've had since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that background hum sound like on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the email from the regional editor that starts with 'As you know, the financial picture remains challenging.' Every reporter on the desk reads that line and starts counting heads. Last spring the hum got loud enough that I updated my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a post was cut, would it be yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not first, because politics is a patch people notice when it's missing. But Priya, who does the weekend shifts, is on a fixed-term contract, and she'd be first. I'd feel guilty being relieved about that.

say: The **transcription tool** is handy for long meetings, and that's about it.
Robots couldn't sit through a three-hour **planning committee** either.
think: My real worry is the **frozen budget**, not AI.
Our regional desk has already shrunk from **nine to six** people.
do: Keep using the **transcription tool** for long council meetings.
Stay active in the **union branch** ahead of the next budget freeze.
Keep saving a **couple of hundred** a month with my partner.
feel: A **low hum** of worry that's been there since I started.
S0.quote: Every frozen budget year means a post on our desk doesn't get filled. Our regional desk has gone from nine people to six.
fieldNote: His pressure is **public funding**, which the plateau does nothing to ease.
Comfortable with **light AI use** and careful to check it, after one bad error.
Names a **fixed-term colleague** as the likely first cut, and admits he'd feel relieved and guilty.

steps.text: Keep using the transcription tool for council meetings
Stay active in the union branch before the next budget round
Save a couple of hundred a month with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say AI can help local news cover more meetings, but only if the savings go back into reporters. I'd say we need rules, so public money doesn't pay for machine-written news with no one checking it. That's a line I could say on air without getting in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the writing-up half of my job goes. A tool can already turn a council transcript into a decent story, and in this picture it gets good enough that management asks why they need me to do it. What's left is the part where I ring a councillor and ask the awkward question, and I'm not sure that's a full-time job on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get properly good at the tools, not just the transcription one, because I'd rather be the reporter who runs the AI tools than the reporter the tools replace. I'd push the union for a deal that time saved goes into more reporting, not fewer reporters. And I'd start a short course in data journalism, which my employer would probably pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. I can see what to do, I just don't know if it's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about it over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my job will probably look very different in two years, and that her job is safer because a robot isn't going to manage thirty seven-year-olds. Lena would laugh and say she'd like to see a robot try. Then we'd talk about whether to wait on buying a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait on the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a year, yes. We'd keep saving for the deposit but not sign anything until I knew where I stood. It's annoying, because we've wanted a place with a garden for ages.

say: AI can help local news, but only if **savings** go back into **reporters**.
**Public money** shouldn't pay for machine-written news that **nobody checks**.
think: The **writing-up half** of my job is likely to go.
Asking councillors the **awkward question** may not be a full-time job on its own.
do: Get properly skilled with the **AI tools**, not just transcription.
Push the union for a deal that saved time goes into **more reporting**.
feel: **Anxious** but not helpless, unsure his plan will be **enough**.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the reporter who runs the AI tools than the reporter the tools replace.
fieldNote: He thinks half his job, the **write-ups**, could go; that's a realistic loss of hours or role.
Mixes a **progressive** union answer with a personal plan to get good at the tools.
The **house purchase** is the first thing he'd put on hold.

steps.text: Learn the newsroom AI writing tools beyond transcription
Push the union for time savings to fund more reporting
Take the employer-paid data journalism course this year
Put off buying a house with Lena for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast for a democracy to handle, and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. I'd be on the union's side in every argument. On air I'd have to stay neutral, but online I'd be much louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm out of a job within two years, along with most of the desk. If a machine can do any thinking work, it can sit through a council meeting, read the budget and write the story, and the broadcaster's budget is too tight to keep people out of kindness. The robots three years later don't matter for me, because almost nothing I do is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the house and keep the deposit as an emergency fund instead. I'd ask Lena's school whether they need teaching assistants, because a classroom is somewhere a person still matters, at least until the robots. And I'd go to every union meeting and lobby the local MP for a proper support scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking of the desk going quiet, one empty chair at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned teaching assistant work. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I've never done it, and the pay is lower than mine. But Lena's head teacher once said they can never find enough people, and I'd rather be useful somewhere than sit at home applying for jobs that don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house dream?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house deposit my partner and I saved would become the money that keeps us afloat while I switch jobs. We'd stay in the rented terrace, which is fine, honestly. I'd feel sad about the garden, but a garden isn't worth a breakdown.

say: This is **far too fast** for a democracy, and government must **cushion** it.
On air I'd stay **neutral**, but online I'd back the **union** loudly.
think: I'm probably **out of a job** within two years, with most of the desk.
Robots arriving later **doesn't help**, because almost none of my work is hands-on.
do: Turn the **house deposit** into an emergency fund.
Ask my partner's school about **teaching assistant** work.
Go to every **union meeting** and lobby the local MP for support.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing the desk going quiet one **empty chair** at a time.
S2.quote: The house deposit my partner and I saved would become the money that keeps us afloat while I switch jobs.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** within two years; the house fund becomes a lifeline.
Looks for **in-person work**, like a classroom, because robots arrive later than thinking AI.
Has to stay **neutral on air**, which makes his online voice his only public outlet.

steps.text: Turn the house deposit into an emergency fund
Ask Lena's school about teaching assistant jobs
Attend every union meeting about the cuts
Lobby the local MP for a worker support scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exactly the time government needs to set up retraining and income support, and it would be shameful to waste it. I'd say the same at work. Lots of my colleagues would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? Five years gives me time to land somewhere instead of falling. I could be a qualified teacher by 2031, which is about when my job goes. Teaching is part thinking work and part being in a room with kids, so the hands-on robots coming three years later buys me a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for a part-time teacher training route, the kind you do while working. I'd ask my editor for a four-day week to make room for it, and keep using AI at work to get my stories done faster. We'd still save, but more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a plan, so it's the manageable kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you actually want to teach, or is it just safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I've always liked explaining things, that's what local politics reporting is, really. I'd teach citizenship or history, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your editor when you ask for the four-day week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm planning ahead, which is what the station tells its audience to do. She'd probably say yes, because it saves her a day's pay. That's the depressing bit.

say: Five years is exactly the time government needs to set up **retraining** and **income support**.
It would be **shameful** to waste that time.
think: Five years lets me **land somewhere** instead of falling.
Teaching mixes thinking work with **being in a room**, so robots coming later buys more time.
do: Apply for a **part-time teacher** training route in the first year.
Ask my editor for a **four-day week** to make room for it.
Keep using AI to finish **stories faster** in the meantime.
feel: **Anxious**, but the **manageable** kind because there's a plan.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to land somewhere instead of falling. I could be a qualified teacher by 2031, which is about when my job goes.
fieldNote: Treats the five years as a **training window**, not a reprieve.
Thinks about the **thinking-then-robots** gap for his next job, not just his current one.
The **four-day week** idea shows he's willing to trade pay for a safer future.

steps.text: Apply for a part-time teacher training route this year
Ask the editor for a four-day week to study
Use AI tools to write council stories faster
Campaign for government retraining and income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to share the gains fairly, with shorter weeks and retraining for everyone. At work I'd say let's plan for this together instead of pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a decade means I can have a proper career in journalism first and still switch. I'd be thirty-seven. Lena keeps saying I'd be a good teacher, so maybe the slow version just gives me the push without the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for at least five years, get good with AI, and maybe buy the house after all. Around year five I'd start teacher training. The union stuff carries on as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's some excitement in it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Excitement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. If AI does the dull summarising, maybe my next few years of reporting are more fun, with more time out talking to people. That's the bit I'd enjoy while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the house in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, with a smaller mortgage than we'd planned, mostly on Lena's salary. Ten years is long enough that waiting would just mean paying rent for nothing. We'd want the garden.

say: Ten years is plenty of time to share the gains with **shorter weeks** and **retraining**.
Let's **plan together** instead of pretending this isn't coming.
think: A decade means I can have a **proper career** first and still switch.
My partner thinks I'd be a **good teacher**, and this gives me the push without panic.
do: Keep **reporting** for at least five years while getting good with AI.
Buy the **house** with a smaller mortgage, mostly on my partner's salary.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with some **excitement** about more time out reporting.
S4.quote: If AI does the dull summarising, maybe my next few years of reporting are more fun, with more time out talking to people.
fieldNote: Still expects the **job to go** eventually, so the worry stays real.
Finds some **excitement** in AI freeing him from summarising, a hopeful note others may not share.
The **house** comes back on the table once the timeline is long.

steps.text: Keep reporting council politics for at least five years
Learn AI tools to cut summarising time
Buy a house with a garden on a smaller mortgage
Start teacher training around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to train for anything and the whole desk goes at once. What would help is paid retraining, so I could study to be a teacher without us losing the house money. Some sort of income support during the switch would make it bearable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to local democracy. If no reporter is sitting in the council chamber, councillors can do what they like. I'd want someone to keep the reporting going even if it isn't me.

headlineQuote: If no reporter is sitting in the council chamber, councillors can do what they like.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** local politics reporter for a regional public broadcaster's website and radio.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly transcription, and always checks it after one bad error.
He and his partner Lena, a **primary teacher**, rent a terrace and save towards a house.
His worries start with a **frozen budget** and grow as AI takes the writing-up half of his job.
In the AGI pictures he plans a move into **teaching**, timed by how many years he gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the whole desk would go with no time to **retrain**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and **income support** so he can switch to teaching.
